cases.abstract: Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA) separates changes in pretrained weight magnitude from low-rank directional updates, giving scale adjustment its own small parameter vector. The design is motivated by a VL-BART analysis in which LoRA's magnitude and direction changes are positively correlated, unlike the negatively correlated changes of full fine-tuning. DoRA normalizes the updated directions and learns their magnitudes separately; the resulting weights can be merged before inference. Across eight commonsense reasoning tasks, LLaMA-7B's average accuracy rises from 74.7% with LoRA to 78.4% with DoRA at the same rank, with trainable fractions of 0.83% and 0.84%. This comparison uses a prior-work LoRA baseline and an adjusted DoRA learning rate. Halving DoRA's rank still yields 77.5% accuracy with 0.43% of parameters trainable, supporting the value of separating magnitude learning under a smaller directional budget. Multimodal averages also improve over LoRA, although VL-BART's video-task average remains below full fine-tuning. Detaching the normalization denominator reduces training overhead: relative to exact normalization, a LLaMA-7B ablation lowers memory by 24.4% with a 0.2-percentage-point accuracy decrease.
cases.methods: DoRA gives column rescaling its own parameters instead of requiring a low-rank matrix update to represent both scale and direction changes. Each adapted column is a learned magnitude multiplied by the normalized sum of the frozen pretrained column and a low-rank update. The magnitude begins at the pretrained column norm, and the low-rank product begins at zero, so adaptation starts from the original model. Normalization assigns scale to the magnitude vector while the factors alter direction. To reduce gradient-graph storage, the implementation recomputes the normalization denominator but detaches it during backpropagation. This retains the forward parameterization and magnitude gradient, while changing the exact direction gradient from a scaled orthogonal projection to scaling alone. After training, the resulting weights can be merged for inference.
cases.results: DoRA's commonsense results indicate that its gains need not come from a larger adaptation budget. On LLaMA-7B, the half-rank configuration achieves 77.5% average accuracy across eight tasks with 0.43% of parameters trainable, exceeding LoRA's 74.7% with 0.83%. At the same rank, DoRA reaches 78.4% with a trainable fraction of 0.84%. The LoRA baseline is imported from prior work, and DoRA's learning rate is adjusted, so these comparisons evaluate the adaptation recipes rather than isolate decomposition under identical optimization. The VL-BART weight analysis is consistent with more independently adjustable components: magnitude-direction correlations are -0.31 for DoRA, -0.62 for full fine-tuning, and 0.83 for LoRA, without establishing the cause of the accuracy gains. This flexibility also does not close every performance gap. VL-BART's reported video-task average rises from 83.5 with LoRA to 85.4 with DoRA but remains below full fine-tuning's 87.5, leaving a gap to training all weights in this setting.
cases.notes: Table 1's same-rank and half-rank comparisons test accuracy at different directional budgets; LLaMA-7B/13B baselines come from prior work, with DoRA learning rates adjusted. Accuracy differences are percentage points, whereas VL-BART's multimodal averages combine different metrics. Figure 2's correlations motivate separation but do not identify the cause of accuracy gains. Section 4.3 and Table 7 distinguish detached normalization from the exact-gradient analysis and support the memory tradeoff. Weight merging removes added adaptation operations at inference; it is not a measured speedup.

cases.abstract: GaLore targets optimizer-state memory without imposing a low-rank parameterization on language-model weights. Its central distinction is that full-rank weights can be updated through compact gradient representations: optimizer statistics are maintained in a projected space, and processed updates are mapped back to the original matrix. Periodically refreshing that space lets accumulated updates span more than one subspace. The analysis provides conditional bounds on gradient stable rank and convergence of projected gradients under fixed projections without adaptive regularization. Experiments examine C4 pretraining and pretrained-model fine-tuning. In a single untuned 7B comparison on 64 A100 GPUs over 19.7 billion tokens, 8-bit GaLore reaches validation perplexity 14.65 versus 14.61 for 8-bit Adam. A separate device-memory measurement combines projection, 8-bit optimizer states, and per-layer updates, requiring 22.0 GB at a token batch size of 256 without offloading or activation checkpointing. This fits within 24 GB capacity. The results support lower-memory full-weight training with near-baseline perplexity in the reported 7B run, but lower throughput in the measured 1B implementation.
cases.methods: GaLore reduces Adam's storage by accumulating moments of a projected gradient rather than of every weight coordinate. For an m-by-n gradient with m <= n, retaining the leading singular vectors yields an m-by-r projector; multiplying by its transpose produces an r-by-n representation. Adam maintains its first and second moments in that smaller space, then the processed update is scaled and mapped back into the full weight matrix. The opposite projection side is used when m > n. Periodic recomputation lets later updates follow different subspaces, so accumulated weight changes are not confined to one rank-r factorization. The formal convergence result concerns fixed projections without adaptive regularization: projected gradients contract when retained-subspace curvature exceeds the continuity-dependent threshold and the learning rate permits contraction. It establishes progress within that subspace, not convergence of the periodically refreshed Adam procedure.
cases.results: At 1B parameters, GaLore preserves much of the full-rank baseline's C4 performance while reducing optimizer storage, rather than shrinking the weight matrix. With rank 512 and 13.1 billion training tokens, validation perplexity is 15.64, compared with 15.56 for full-rank Adam and 19.21 for same-rank LoRA. Estimated weight-and-optimizer storage falls to 4.38 GB, versus 7.80 GB and 6.17 GB, respectively. The quality comparison therefore favors compressing gradient statistics over restricting learned changes to a single low-rank factorization in this setting. The separate 7B device footprint of 22.0 GB also relies on 8-bit states and immediate per-layer updates at a small token batch size; it is not a projection-only saving. A corresponding 1B measurement at 256 tokens makes the runtime tradeoff explicit: memory decreases from 6.93 GB with 8-bit Adam to 5.63 GB with 8-bit GaLore, while throughput falls from 1205.31 to 1019.63 tokens per second. Lower storage thus enables a different memory budget, not faster training in this measurement.
cases.notes: Table 2 supports the 1B quality-and-storage comparison; its memory values estimate weights plus optimizer states, not total device usage. Section 5.3's 7B quality run is one untuned trial on 64 A100 GPUs. Section 5.5's 22.0 GB footprint combines projection, 8-bit states, and per-layer updates; capacity feasibility is not a completed consumer-GPU training run. Table 11 supplies paired 1B throughput and memory values without resolving its ambiguous layer-wise labels. The fixed-projection theorem concerns projected gradients, not switching Adam or full-gradient convergence. Fine-tuning is mixed: GLUE averages remain below full fine-tuning, and LLaMA-7B OpenAssistant perplexity is slightly worse than LoRA's.
